claims.text: Pack-cementation aluminizing of a Mo–Nb–Ta–W refractory high-entropy alloy improves its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The improvement arises from formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale.
The untreated Mo–Nb–Ta–W alloy has no pre-existing protective oxide layer.
An Al-rich pack treatment containing Al powder and activators at 900°C for 10 hours will produce the intended surface modification.
The aluminizing treatment forms an Al-enriched surface layer.
During high-temperature exposure, the Al-enriched surface layer converts into a continuous and adherent Al2O3 barrier.
Deposited Al diffuses into the alloy surface under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Al diffusion results in in-situ formation of a protective alumina scale.
The alumina barrier inhibits oxygen diffusion into the substrate and slows oxidation kinetics.
At 1000°C in 1 atm oxygen for 50 hours, the aluminized alloy will exhibit approximately an 80% reduction in oxidation kinetics relative to untreated samples.
The aluminized alloy will exhibit better oxide-scale adhesion than untreated samples if cementation parameters are optimized.
Untreated Mo–Nb–Ta–W exhibits rapid oxidation at 1000°C in 1 atm oxygen.
Untreated Mo–Nb–Ta–W exhibits poor oxide-scale adherence at 1000°C in 1 atm oxygen.
The treatment's effectiveness is sensitive to pack-cementation parameters.
Adhesion failure or thermal-expansion mismatch can compromise protection during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Prior studies support formation of protective alumina scales through surface aluminizing.
The hypothesis is falsified if treated samples fail to achieve at least a 50% reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to untreated samples.
The hypothesis is also falsified if the treated oxide scale is discontinuous or exhibits significant spallation relative to untreated samples.
